paragraphs.source_en: After about seven minutes, Kangetsu arrived just as promised. Because he was to give a lecture that evening, he had, unusually, put on a handsome frock coat; with his freshly laundered high white collar, his masculine good looks were improved by about twenty percent, and he greeted them with perfect composure: “I am a little late.” Meitei looked at the master and said, “The two of us have been waiting for ages. Let us begin at once. What do you say, Kushami?” The master, having no choice, gave a lukewarm “Mm.” But Kangetsu was in no hurry and said, “Please pour me a glass of water first.” Meitei alone made a fuss, saying, “Well, so you really mean to do this in full formal style. Next you will be asking us for applause.” Kangetsu took his manuscript from the inside pocket of his formal coat and first, with deliberate calm, offered a preface: “Since this is a rehearsal, I ask you to criticize me without reserve.” Then he began his lecture:

paragraphs.source_en: “The punishment of criminals by hanging is a method practiced chiefly among the Anglo-Saxon peoples. If we go further back into antiquity, hanging was chiefly carried out as a method of suicide. It is said that among the Jews the custom was to kill criminals by throwing stones at them. When one studies the Old Testament, the word ‘hanging’ appears to mean hanging up the criminal’s corpse to be food for wild beasts or carnivorous birds. According to Herodotus, even before leaving Egypt the Jews seem to have deeply detested exposing corpses at night. The Egyptians, after beheading a criminal, nailed only the torso to a cross and exposed it by night. And the Persians...” “Kangetsu, you are drifting farther and farther away from hanging. Is that all right?” Meitei interrupted. “I am just about to enter the main subject, so please be patient a little longer... Now then, what of the Persians? They too seem to have used crucifixion in executions. However, whether they fastened the criminal up alive, or nailed him up after killing him, is not quite clear...”
